Variants.Content: Fozo is not a southern-style noble family that relies on a fixed territory to continue, but a khalasar composed of relatives, bandits, bloodriders and ordinary riders on the sea of ​​​​grass. Horses are not only wealth, food, and status, but also a measure of migration speed and military strength. Any leader who squanders his horses, misjudges water sources, or allows the spoils to flow only to a few close associates will damage his prestige. The tradition of Fodro I is preserved by campfire stories, mothers' teachings, and the experiences of riders, and does not need a stone tablet to exist. It can pass through different roads, accept different visitors, and even reunite after failure, but its obedience must always be determined by whether it can survive together.

The riders of Fozhuo look at a leader and first see how he treats his own horses, and then see how he distributes the enemy's horses. Those who mistreat their mounts will be looked down upon, while those who monopolize the spoils will find that the team behind them is getting shorter and shorter.

Those in the camp who sew saddles, boil milk, and take care of young children know that the khalasar is not just composed of charges. If Buddha allows these nameless labors to be fed and protected, the singing will continue after the warriors leave the camp.

The merchants and guards at the edge of the Grass Sea will not regard Fo Zhuo as a permanently fixed flag. They observe whether the horses are tired and whether there are quarrels among the troops, because the inside story of a khalasar is often more reliable than the friendship told by Kaa.
